body.p: U
UCAL*

Disciple of Agur, the wise man whose sayings are recorded in the book of Proverbs (Prv 30:1; see nlt mg). The meaning of the passage is obscure. Many have suggested that the names Itiel (Ithiel) and Ukal (Ucal) are not proper nouns but should be translated, “I am weary and worn out, O God.”
UEL
Bani’s descendant and a priest who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife during the postexilic era (Ezr 10:34).
UGARIT*

City in northwest Aram (Syria) during the second millennium BC. Though the city is not mentioned in the Bible, it is a significant archaeological site that illuminates OT language and history. Ugarit was located just east of the Mediterranean coast, approximately 175 miles (281.6 kilometers) north of Tsor (Tyre).

Being known previously only from the Amarna letters, the ruins of Ugarit were discovered accidentally by a peasant farmer in 1928. The resulting discoveries were among the most important in the 20th century. Since Ugarit was a political and cultural center, its scribes created and transcribed documents in a wide variety of Near Eastern languages, including a language closely related to Hebrew that was written in an alphabetic cuneiform script. The discovery and subsequent deciphering of “Ugaritic” has influenced biblical studies both linguistically and culturally. Ugaritic has illuminated some otherwise obscure Hebrew passages and given greater attestation to others. For instance, the terms used to describe each of the various sacrificial offerings are very similar in Hebrew and Ugaritic, though the sacrificial systems themselves vary quite dramatically. Hebrew and Ugaritic poetry are quite similar stylistically, thus assisting in the understanding of Hebrew verse and also increasing the appreciation of its ancient heritage. Books like Iyov (Job) that often have been dated late by biblical critics exhibit significant Ugaritic parallels in style, vocabulary, and occasionally in literary allusion as well.

Perhaps the most significant contribution derived from the study of Ugaritic texts and cultural artifacts is the improved understanding of Kena’ani (Canaanite) culture and religion. The Ugaritic texts provide justification for the strongly negative assessment of Kena’ani culture given in the Bible. Three principal religious epics have been discovered in the Ugaritic corpus, written in honor of Keret, Aqhat, and Ba’al (Baal), respectively. The Ba’al epic describes the way in which Ba’al becomes lord of the earth after battling Yam, the god of the sea. The epics further reveal a great deal about Kena’ani religious ritual, reinforcing biblical contentions concerning the sexual permissiveness and degradation of the society. The strong biblical injunctions against the worship of Ba’al and the Asherahs and the command to utterly destroy the Kena’anim (Canaanites) are more easily understood in the context of the Ugaritic religious epics.

Finally, the Ugaritic texts potentially illuminate some historical questions relating to the OT. For instance, when Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) was sick with a boil, he was instructed by Yeshayah (Isaiah) to treat it with a poultice of figs (2 Kgs 20:7; Is 38:21). This procedure is attested to in a Ugaritic text that prescribes it as a treatment for boils that infected horses.
See also Inscriptions.
ULAI

River near the Persian capital city of Shushan (Susa) where Daniyel (Daniel) received a vision concerning the end times (Dn 8:2-16). It is likely the same as the Eulaeus, which is described by both Greek and Roman geographers as a stream that flowed to the west of the citadel of Shushan.
ULAM
1. Clan in Menasheh’s (Manasseh’s) tribe (1 Chr 7:16-17).
2. Eshek’s firstborn son and a mighty warrior in Benyamin’s (Benjamin’s) tribe (1 Chr 8:39-40).
ULCER*
See Sore.
ULLA
Family in Asher’s tribe (1 Chr 7:39).
UMMAH

One of the villages inherited by Asher’s tribe after the conquest of Kena’an (Canaan) (Jos 19:30). Neither the location of Umah (Ummah) nor the accompanying villages (Afek (Aphek) and Rehov (Rehob)) are known.
UNCIRCUMCISION*

Natural condition of the male, that is, with the foreskin covering his penis. Since the Yehudim (Jews), among many other peoples, surgically removed this as a sign of their covenant with God (Gn 17:9-14; Ex 12:48; Lv 12:3), the term came to designate “non-Jew” or “Gentile” (Pelishtim (Philistines), Greeks, and Romans did not circumcise, but Mitsrim (Egyptians) and many Semitic peoples did). By extension, it connoted “those outside the covenant.”

The term “uncircumcision” occurs 20 times in the NT, most of the time meaning simply “Gentile,” as opposed to Yehudi (Jew). Paulos (Paul) argues strongly against making such distinctions. For Paulos, the attitude of one’s heart toward God is much more important than ritual law, which has nothing to do with his salvation (Rom 2:25-27). Avraham (Abraham) became a believer and was justified by God while he was uncircumcised, so circumcision has nothing to do with his salvation (3:30; 4:9-12). Formerly, Gentiles were excluded from the people of God (Eph 2:11-12), but now Jewish and gentile believers have become one in Christ (Gal 2:7; 5:6; 6:15; Col 3:11). Paulos refuses to give way to those demanding circumcision for full church membership.

In one passage (Col 2:8-15), Paulos speaks of uncircumcision metaphorically, meaning a person’s unregenerate state. Here uncircumcision is equivalent to “the flesh” (meaning one’s evil impulse or natural state). As literal flesh is cut away in the rite of circumcision, so this “flesh” is cut away by Christ at the time of conversion, as symbolized in baptism. The baptized person is one purified from “uncleanness” as a circumcised Gentile is purified from previous uncircumcised uncleanness.
See also Circumcision.
UNCLEAN, UNCLEANNESS
See Cleanness and Uncleanness, Regulations Concerning.
UNFORGIVABLE SIN*
See Unpardonable Sin, The.
UNICORN*

KJV rendering for an animal called a “wild ox” in the nlt and most modern translations (Nm 24:8; Dt 33:17). Unicorn is an unfortunate translation (following the Septuagint) because the animal had two horns, not one. See Animals (Wild Ox).
UNLEAVENED BREAD

Bread made without leaven (yeast). In ancient times, bread makers used a piece of dough remaining from a former baking process, a piece that had fermented and developed a certain acid content—the yeast that caused bread to rise.

Bread used at the Jewish Passover and most other religious observances was, by the command of God, unleavened (Ex 12:15-20; 23:15). Only under certain conditions were the people permitted to use leavened bread for spiritual purposes (Lv 7:13; 23:17). This was largely owing to the fact that leaven generally symbolized evil; fermentation implied decay and corruption.

With the exception of Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) teaching on the kingdom of God (Mt 13:33), the NT also speaks of leaven with a negative connotation. Yeshua warned of the leaven of the Farisaios (Pharisees) and Saddoukaios (Sadducees) (16:6); Paulos (Paul) exhorted believers to guard against that tiny bit of yeast—unhealthy values—that can work through a whole batch of dough (1 Cor 5:6-8).
See also Bread; Food and Food Preparation; Leaven.
UNLEAVENED BREAD, Festival of
See Feasts and Festivals of Israel.
UNNI
1. One of the musicians appointed by the chief of the Levites to sing and play the harp as part of the temple service during David’s reign (1 Chr 15:18-20).
2. KJV spelling of Unno in Nehemiah 12:9. See Unno.
UNNO*
One of the Levites who participated in the temple service during the postexilic era (Neh 12:9).
UNPARDONABLE SIN*, The
Attributing to Satan what is actually the work of the Holy Spirit as demonstrated through Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ. This sin is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.

The unpardonable sin must be defined by its context, which is found in Matthew 12:31-32 and Mark 3:28-30. In these passages, Yeshua had just cast a demon from a man who was blind and mute. Incontrovertible evidence of the power of God had just occurred. But the Farisaios (Pharisees), with stubborn unbelief, credited this display of God’s power to Beelzebul, the devil (Mt 12:24). Several Scriptures reveal that many Yehudim (Jews) had expressed the same kind of fallacious opinion, namely, that Yeshua was performing miracles by the power of the devil (Mt 9:34; 11:18; Lk 7:33; 11:14-20; Jn 7:20; 8:48, 52; 10:20). A group of Yehudim, mostly Farisaios, were guilty of attributing to the devil what was the work of the Spirit demonstrated through the Lord Yeshua. They committed the unpardonable sin when they said that Yeshua’s actions, performed by the power of the Holy Spirit, originated from Beelzebul, the devil. Put simply, they sinned grievously by boldly characterizing Yeshua’s work as coming from the devil. Interestingly, many Yehudim perpetuated this false characterization about Yeshua long after his death. They did not deny that he did miracles; they said he did miracles by the power of the devil.
What Isn’t the Unpardonable Sin

The unpardonable sin is not Yisrael’s (Israel’s) rebellion against God, even though this rebellion resulted in the eternal judgment of thousands and a temporary elimination of God’s blessing. The “sin unto death” mentioned by Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) (1 Jn 5:16-17) is not the unpardonable sin. It would be impossible for a person who has redemption and the forgiveness of sin (Eph 1:7), cleansing for present and future sin (1 Jn 1:7), and eternal life (Jn 3:16) to commit an unpardonable sin. But those who commit the “sin unto death” are all Christians. First John 5:16 says the person who commits the “sin unto death” is a “brother” in Christ.

The unpardonable sin is not rejection of the Lord Yeshua, until the rejecter dies in his unbelief. Such a sin will not be forgiven throughout eternity, but it is not the same sin as that which Yeshua condemned with these words: “Anyone who blasphemes against me, the Son of Man, can be forgiven, but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven, either in this world or in the world to come” (Mt 12:32, nlt). Numerous passages repeat the warning that unbelief in the Savior results in eternal death (Jn 3:18, 36; 1 Jn 5:12; Rv 20:15; 21:8), but these Scriptures do not directly speak of the unpardonable sin. Yeshua asserted that a person could be an unbeliever in him, even to the degree of speaking against him, yet not be guilty of the unpardonable sin.
See also Justification, Justified; Sin unto Death.
UPHARSIN*
Aramaic word interpreted as “divided” in Daniel 5:25 (kjv). See Mene, Mene, Tekel, Parsin.
UPHAZ
Region well known for its gold (Jer 10:9; Dn 10:5). Some contend that Ufaz (Uphaz) is a scribal error for Ofir (Ophir) (only one consonant is different), another region famous for its fine gold.
See also Ophir (Place).
UPPER GATE

One of the gates leading to the temple mount in Yerushalem (Jerusalem). It was built by Yotam (Jotham) (2 Kgs 15:35; 2 Chr 27:3) and served as the principal access between the royal palace and the temple area (2 Chr 23:20; Ez 9:2).
UPPER ROOM

Second-story room of a Hebrew or a Greek house; often like a tower, built on the flat roof of a Hebrew home for privacy, for comfort during the hot season, or for the entertainment of guests. In some instances it could accommodate large gatherings of people. In at least one instance, the room was on the third story (Acts 20:8). Eutukos (Eutychus), sitting in the window, went to sleep and fell three stories to the street below (vv 9-10). It may have been a similar type of accident that caused Ahazyah’s (Ahaziah’s) fatal injury when he fell through the latticework of his upper room (2 Kgs 1:2).

Eliyah (Elijah) took the dead son of the widow of Tserefat (Zarephath) to an upper room where he had been staying and raised him from the dead (1 Kgs 17:19-23). David went to an upper room for privacy to mourn the death of Avshalom (Absalom) (2 Sm 18:33). The kings of Yehudah (Judah) built strange altars near the upper room of Ahaz, which Yoshiyah (Josiah) pulled down as part of his reform program (2 Kgs 23:12).

Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) ate the Passover supper in an upper room with his disciples (Mk 14:15; Lk 22:12). The size of some of these rooms is evident from the fact that, after Yeshua had left and ascended to heaven, the disciples went to the upper room where they all had been staying before. The congregation attending the meeting in Troias (Troas) was not a small one either (Acts 20:8). Dorkas (Dorcas) was laid in an upper room after she had died; later, Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) was taken up to the same room to pray for her restoration to life (Acts 9:36-41).
See also Architecture; Homes and Dwellings.
UR (Person)
Father of Elifal (Eliphal), one of David’s mighty men (1 Chr 11:35); probably the same as Ahasbay (Ahasbai) in the parallel passage (2 Sm 23:34).
UR (Place)

Hometown of Terah, the father of Avraham (Abraham), and the birthplace of Avraham and Sarah. It is mentioned by name only four times in the Bible (Gn 11:28, 31; 15:7; Neh 9:7), always with the full name “Ur of the Kasdim (Chaldeans).”

The modern site is known as Tell el Muqayyar, “The Mound of Bitumen.” The results of archaeological investigations demonstrate that Avraham came from a great city, cultured, sophisticated, and powerful. The landscape was dominated by the ziggurat, or temple tower, and the life of the city was controlled by a religion with a multiplicity of gods. The chief deity was Nannar, or Sin, the moon god, who was also worshiped at Haran. Near his ziggurat was a temple dedicated to his consort, the moon goddess, Ningal.

Many clay tablets found at Ur tell of the business life of the city, which focused on the temples and their income. There were factories here, such as the weaving establishment for the manufacture of woolen cloth. Some tablets dealt with religion, history, law, and education. Students were instructed in reading and writing in cuneiform script. They were taught multiplication and division, and some were even able to extract square roots and cube roots.

Domestic architecture was highly developed. Houses had two stories and many rooms (10 to 20), sometimes with a private chapel. Small clay religious figures (teraphim or household idols) were discovered. Many art objects made of precious metals and other costly materials have been excavated, especially in the royal tombs. These tombs also contained the remains of a number of retainers who must have been put to death at the time of the royal burials in order to accompany their masters in the afterlife.
URBANUS
Believer greeted as one of Paulos’s (Paul’s) coworkers in Christ (Rom 16:9).
URI
1. Father of Betsalel (Bezalel) from Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe, and a builder of the tabernacle (Ex 31:2; 35:30; 38:22; 1 Chr 2:20; 2 Chr 1:5).
2. Father of Gever (Geber), one of Shelomoh’s (Solomon’s) officers in Gilead (1 Kgs 4:19).
3. One of the temple gatekeepers who put away his foreign wife at Ezra’s request (Ezr 10:24).
URIAH

1. Hiti (Hittite) who joined the people of Yisrael (Israel), became a leader in David’s army, and was listed among the king’s mighty men (2 Sm 23:39; 1 Chr 11:41). Uriyah’s (Uriah’s) wife was Bat-Sheva (Bathsheba), with whom David committed adultery while Uriyah was fighting the Amonim (Ammonites). Upon learning that she was pregnant, David summoned Uriyah to Yerushalem (Jerusalem), hoping that Uriyah would sleep with his wife and consider himself the child’s father. However, Uriyah slept in the servants’ quarters because he was unwilling to enjoy the comforts of home while his companions were at war. The second night David again tried to entice him to sleep with his wife. Even after falling into a drunken stupor, Uriyah still could not be persuaded to go home; instead, he spent the night at the palace. To deepen the intrigue, David sent Uriyah back to the battle, ordering him positioned at a vulnerable place, where he was killed (2 Sm 11; Mt 1:6).
See also David; Genealogy of Jesus Christ.
2. Priest who built an altar at Yerushalem in imitation of an Assyrian model at King Ahaz of Yehudah’s (Judah’s) request (2 Kgs 16:10-16).

3. Priest who was the father of Meremot (Meremoth). Meremot weighed the silver, gold, and vessels for the temple (Ezr 8:33) and built portions of the Yerushalem wall during the days of Nehemyah (Nehemiah) (Neh 3:4, 21).
4. One of the men who stood to Ezra’s right when Ezra read the law to the people (Neh 8:4). He is perhaps the same man as #3 above.
5. Priest whom Yeshayah (Isaiah) took as a witness (Is 8:2). He is perhaps the same man as #2 above.

6. Prophet and Shemayah’s (Shemaiah’s) son from Kiryat-Yearim (Kiriath-jearim). Uriyah enraged King Yehoyakim (Jehoiakim) by prophesying against Yehudah and Yerushalem. Fearing for his life, Uriyah fled to Mitsrayim (Egypt) but was eventually abducted and brought back to King Yehoyakim, who subsequently put him to death (Jer 26:20-23).
URIAS*
KJV spelling (in Matthew 1:6) of Uriyah (Uriah), Bat-Sheva’s (Bathsheba’s) husband, whom David had killed. See Uriah #1.
URIEL
1. Levite of the Kohatite (Kohathite) branch who is listed as the son of Tahat (Tahath) and the father of Uziyah (Uzziah) (1 Chr 6:24).

2. Levite who officiated over the moving of the ark from the house of Oved-Edom (Obed-edom) to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (1 Chr 15:5-11). He was a Kohatite clan chief in charge of 120 men who participated in the ceremony, and he was personally sanctified for the purpose of carrying the ark.

3. Grandfather of King Aviyah (Abijah) of Yehudah (Judah), and the father of the queen mother, Ma’akah (Maacah) (Hebrew Micaiah), the favored wife of Rehav’am (Rehoboam) (2 Chr 13:2). There is potential difficulty in that Avshalom (Absalom) is also called the father of Mikayah (Micaiah) (Ma’akah) in 2 Chronicles 11:20. Josephus explained this discrepancy by suggesting that Ma’akah’s mother may have been Avshalom’s daughter Tamar, so that Uriel would be the father of Ma’akah and Avshalom the maternal grandfather. While many adopt this suggestion, others have posited that Avshalom was known by two different names, particularly after he had been disgraced.
URIJAH*
KJV spelling of Uriyah (Uriah). See Uriah #2–4, 6.
URIM AND THUMMIM

Two untranslated Hebrew words that might mean “lights and perfections.” They refer to some kind of stones or tokens that the ancient high priests of Yisrael (Israel) used for discovering the will of God (Nm 27:21). They were probably like dice or coins that had to land upright or upside down. According to Exodus 28:30, they were kept on or in the breastpiece of the high priest. They are not mentioned from the time of Sha’ul (Saul) (1 Sm 28:6) until the time of Ezra and Nehemyah (Nehemiah) (Ezr 2:63; Neh 7:65), when they were used for reaccrediting returned priests. In 1 Samuel 14:41 (rsv, niv mg, nlt mg), the Greek translation preserves what may have been lost from the Hebrew original, a mention of them in connection with Sha’ul’s effort to determine guilt in his army. That they could give answers to true-false or yes-no questions is evident from this verse. Hence, the system was probably akin to casting lots.

None of the major spiritual leaders (e.g., Avraham (Abraham), Mosheh (Moses), David, or the prophets) ever used them for determining the will of God, and there is no mention of them in the NT. The Urim and Tumim (Thummim) belonged to the nation Yisrael in its developing years, not when there were prophets and surely not once the Holy Spirit was available to believers.
See also Lots, Casting of.
UTHAI
1. One who returned to Yisrael (Israel) following the exile. He is listed as the son of Amihud (Ammihud) from the Perets (Perez) branch of Yehudah’s (Judah’s) tribe (1 Chr 9:4).
2. One of Bigvay’s (Bigvai’s) sons who returned to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) with Ezra (Ezr 8:14).
UZ (Person)

1. Aram’s firstborn son and a descendant of Shem (Gn 10:23). In the parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 1:17, Uts (Uz) is linked directly to Shem without mention of Aram. He is perhaps the forefather of the Aramean nation situated in the Arami (Syrian) desert regions.
2. Firstborn son of Avraham’s (Abraham’s) brother Nahor by his concubine, Milkah (Milcah) (Gn 22:21).
3. Son of Dishan and the grandson of Se’ir (Seir) the Hori (Horite) (Gn 36:28; 1 Chr 1:42).
UZ (Place)

Homeland of Iyov (Job) (Jb 1:1). The name appears in parallels with Edom and is associated with the Uts (Uz) in the family tree of the original Horim (Horites) in Se’ir (Seir) (Lam 4:21). The book of Iyov does not locate the land of Uts, but it does say that the sons of the East (Kedem) lived there (Jb 1:3). Uts is also said to be close to the desert (v 15) and to the Chasdim (v 17). This indicates that it was located to the east of the land of Yisrael (Israel).

The associations with Edom strongly suggest that the land of Uts was populated by descendants of the Horim of Se’ir. Further support for this view is a verse in the Greek version at the end of the book of Iyov: “since he had lived in the land of Uts on the borders of Edom and Arav (Arabia).” Certain ancient traditions place the home of Iyov in Bashan. Josephus also says that Iyov lived in Traconitis and Damesek (Damascus) (Antiquities 1.6.4), with reference to the Uts of the Aramean genealogy (Gn 10:23).
UZAI
Father of Palal, a repairer of the Yerushalem (Jerusalem) wall during Nehemyah’s (Nehemiah’s) day (Neh 3:25).
UZAL (Person)
Son of Yaketan (Joktan), a descendant of Ever (Eber) through Shem’s line (Gn 10:27; 1 Chr 1:21).
UZAL (Place)
Place mentioned with Dan and Yavan (Javan) in an obscure passage (Ez 27:19); it is identifiable with modern Sana (ancient Awzal), the capital of Yemen.
UZZA

1. Owner or initial planter of a garden that served as the burial place for kings Menasheh (Manasseh) and Amon of Yehudah (Judah) (2 Kgs 21:18, 26). The “garden of Uza (Uzza)” was apparently adjacent to Menasheh’s royal residence.
2. KJV spelling for Uza, Shimei’s son, in 1 Chronicles 6:29. See Uzzah #2.
3. Son or descendant of Ehud from Benyamin’s (Benjamin’s) tribe (1 Chr 8:7), listed as an ancestor of Mordekai (Mordecai) in extrabiblical texts.
4. KJV spelling for Uza, Avinadav’s (Abinadab’s) son, in 1 Chronicles 13:7-11. See Uzzah #1.
5. Forefather of a family of temple servants who returned to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) with Zerubavel (Zerubbabel) following the exile (Ezr 2:49; Neh 7:51).
UZZAH

1. Son of Avinadav (Abinadab) who was killed while accompanying the cart that carried the ark of the covenant when it was returned from the Pelishtim (Philistines) (2 Sm 6:1-8; 1 Chr 13:7-11). He was struck dead by the Lord because he took hold of the ark while trying to steady it, thereby violating the instructions of Numbers 4:15. Uza’s (Uzzah’s) brother, Ahyo (Ahio), was apparently leading the oxen while Uza walked alongside. As a result of the incident, David renamed the site Perets-Uza (Perez-uzzah) (“the breaking forth against Uza”) and left the ark at the home of Oved-Edom (Obed-edom).
2. Levite from the clan of Merari who is listed as the son of Shimei and the father of Shimea (1 Chr 6:29).
UZZEN-SHEERAH
Town built by She’erah (Sheerah), who was either the daughter or granddaughter of Efrayim (Ephraim) (1 Chr 7:24).
UZZI

1. Descendant of Eliezer who was in the direct ancestral line of high priests, though he apparently never served in that capacity (1 Chr 6:5-6, 51). He is listed as the son of Buki (Bukki) and the father of Zerahyah (Zerahiah); he was a lineal ancestor of Tsadok (Zadok) and later Ezra (Ezr 7:4).
2. Clan chief and mighty warrior of the tribe of Yisakar (Issachar). He was one of the six sons of Tola and the father of Yizrahyah (Izrahiah), his successor as clan chief (1 Chr 7:2-3).
3. Clan chief and mighty warrior of Benyamin’s (Benjamin’s) tribe, listed as one of the sons of Bela (1 Chr 7:7).
4. Head of one of the Benyamini (Benjaminite) clans that returned from Bavel (Babylon), listed as the son of Micri and the father of Elah (1 Chr 9:8).
5. One of the overseers of the Levites in Yerushalem (Jerusalem), listed as the son of Bani from the clan of Asaf (Asaph) (Neh 11:22).
6. Head of the priestly house of Yedayah (Jedaiah) during the days of Yoyakim (Joiakim) the high priest (Neh 12:19).
7. One of the priests (or Levites) who participated in the dedication of the rebuilt temple (Neh 12:42). He may be the same as #5 or #6 above.
UZZIA
One of David’s mighty men (1 Chr 11:44). He was described as an Ashterati (Ashterathite), which probably means that he was from Ashtarot (Ashtaroth), a town on the east side of the Yarden (Jordan).
UZZIAH

1. Yehudah’s (Judah’s) king from around 792 to 740 BC (cf. 2 Kgs 14:21-22; 15:1-7; 2 Chr 26:1-23), the son of King Amatsyah (Amaziah) and Yekaleyah (Jecoliah) of Yerushalem (Jerusalem). Uziyah (Uzziah) is the name he is called in Chronicles, but in Kings he is known as Azaryah (Azariah). Azaryah means “the Lord has helped”; the meaning of Uziyah is “my strength is the Lord.” Azaryah may have been his given name and Uziyah a throne name taken upon his accession. He came to the throne at the age of 16, after the death of his father, who was assassinated in Lakish (Lachish) as a result of a conspiracy arising from his apostasy.

Uziyah was a capable, energetic, and well-organized person, with many diverse interests. The Lord blessed him in all of his undertakings, so that he prospered. He is characterized as one who “did what was right in the eyes of the Lord” (2 Kgs 15:3; 2 Chr 26:4). He determined to seek God and went to Zekaryah (Zechariah) (not the postexilic prophet) for spiritual instruction. Consequently, “as long as he sought Yahweh, God made him prosper” (2 Chr 26:5).

The prophets of the Lord were active during his reign. Yeshayah (Isaiah), Hoshea (Hosea), and Amos began their prophetic work in the time of Uziyah (Is 1:1; Hos 1:1; Am 1:1). Uziyah was also active with military campaigns. His primary success was against Yisrael’s (Israel’s) strong historical enemy, the Pelishtim (Philistines). He broke down the walls of Gat (Gath), Yavneh (Jabneh), and Ashdod and built his own cities in Peleshet (Philistia). He also built many fortifications, such as fortified towers in Yerushalem and in the wilderness. He defeated some Arabs and also the Meunim (Meunites), and he brought the Amonim (Ammonites) under tribute (2 Chr 27:5-8). Uziyah had an army “fit for war,” which was drafted according to census and organized into divisions. There were 2,600 officers and 307,500 fighting men who could wage war with mighty power. The army was well outfitted, with weapons, such as spears, bows, and sling stones, and with defensive equipment, including shields, helmets, and coats of armor (2 Chr 26:14). Second Chronicles 26:15 describes a kind of catapult, which was to be stationed on the towers and at the corners of walls for defensive purposes. This type of weapon could hurl arrows or large stones. Through his achievements and especially his military power, he became famous.

But Uziyah had a sad downfall. As Proverbs 16:18 says, pride goes before a fall. His pride became clearly evident when he presumed the function of a priest. When he entered the temple to offer incense on the altar of incense, he was confronted for his presumptuous behavior by Azaryah the priest and 80 other priests. When Uziyah became angry, the Lord struck him with leprosy, so that he was forced to live in isolation and could not enter the temple. His son, Yotam (Jotham), became acting head of state and then succeeded to the kingship at the time of Uziyah’s death.
2. Kohatite (Kohathite) Levite and forefather of Shmuel (Samuel) (1 Chr 6:24).
3. Father of Yonatan (Jonathan), David’s treasurer (1 Chr 27:25).
4. One of Harim’s five sons who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife during the postexilic period (Ezr 10:21; 1 Esd 9:21).
5. Descendant of Perets (Perez) from Yehudah’s tribe (Neh 11:4).
UZZIEL

1. Youngest of the sons of Kohat (Kohath) of Levi’s tribe, who became the head of the Uzieli (Uzzielite) division of the Kohatites (Kohathites) (Ex 6:18; Nm 3:19, 27, 30; 1 Chr 26:23). He was Aharon’s (Aaron’s) uncle, and his sons, Mishael and Elitsafan (Elzaphan), carried Nadav (Nadab) and Avihu (Abihu) out of the camp when they rebelled against Aharon’s authority (Ex 6:22; Lv 10:4). Several of his descendants were significant during Yisrael’s (Israel’s) history, including Aminadav (Amminadab), who officiated over David’s transfer of the ark to Yerushalem (Jerusalem), and Mikah (Micah) and Yishiyah (Isshiah), who were chiefs among the Levites during the reign of Shelomoh (Solomon) (1 Chr 15:10; 23:20).

2. Son of Yishei (Ishi) who was one of the leaders of the Shim’oni (Simeonite) warriors who defeated the Amonim (Ammonites) at Se’ir (Seir) during the reign of Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) (1 Chr 4:42). As a result of defeating the Amalekim (Amalekites), who had not been defeated earlier by Sha’ul (Saul) or David, the Simeonites inherited the land.
3. Benyamini (Benjaminite) clan chief who is listed as the son of Bela, the son of Benyamin (Benjamin) (1 Chr 7:7).
4. Son of Heyman (Heman) of the Levite clan of Asaf (Asaph) (1 Chr 25:4). A variant name is Azarel (v 18, nlt mg).
5. Levite who participated in the reconsecration of the temple under Hizkiyah (2 Chr 29:14), listed as the son of Yedutun (Jeduthun).

6. Goldsmith who worked on rebuilding the gates of Yerushalem (Neh 3:8). His name indicates that he was likely a priest who had the responsibility of making and repairing the temple instruments and vessels (cf. 1 Chr 9:29).
